Chapter Two: How Ordinary People Become Part of Something Unthinkable
Imagine months dragging on, each one feeling heavier than the last. At first, soldiers joked about heading home soon, but reality set in—their tours would stretch out much longer than anyone hoped. That early sense of purpose? It started to slip away, replaced by exhaustion... and a frustration that just wouldn’t go away.
Out there, the enemy seemed to be everywhere—and nowhere. Every civilian could be a threat. Every shadow might hide something dangerous.
Under this constant pressure, the demand for results only grew. Commanders needed information—names, locations, plans. The safety of the entire unit depended on knowing what the enemy might do next. So interrogations happened more often, and the line between honest questioning and straight-up coercion? It started to blur.
Some soldiers, desperate to protect their friends or prove themselves, pushed much harder than they should have. Others just watched, uneasy, as the boundaries slowly shifted.
One night, a group of soldiers brought in a man they suspected of planting bombs. He was terrified—shaking, barely able to speak English. The interrogator that night wasn’t some hardened officer, just a peer—someone who never imagined he’d end up in this position.
He felt the weight of it all. He remembered friends’ faces, friends who’d been hurt by roadside bombs. The urge to get answers was overwhelming.
At first, he tried to do everything by the book—asking questions, offering water, trying to build a little trust. But when the man refused to talk, frustration crept in. And that’s when things started to shift.
The questions turned into shouting. Then came threats. And eventually, physical force.
Most people don’t even notice when the line is crossed. It happens in tiny steps—a shove instead of a gentle push, a slap where there used to be just a warning. Every time, it feels justified. The mission’s too important. The risks are just too high. Suddenly, the rules that were supposed to protect everyone start to feel like obstacles.
And when nobody steps in to stop it, that new “normal” takes hold.
For a lot of folks, the first time was the hardest. After that, it got easier to justify. They’d remind themselves—the enemy’s dangerous. He’d do the same to us.
That sense of right and wrong, the moral clarity that used to guide them, faded away. It got replaced by this grim, practical mindset. The war was changing them, in ways they didn’t even fully realize.
Meanwhile, back home, families and friends had no idea. Letters and phone calls were full of reassurances—little stories about the weather, about missing home, maybe even a joke about the food. No one talked about the things that haunted them at night—the shame, the guilt, that nagging fear about who they were becoming.
It was just easier to pretend nothing had changed.
But deep down, most of them knew. Something important was slipping away. The person they’d been before the war? That version of themselves was starting to feel like a stranger.
